evals.prompt: I want to build a plant-care app: you snap a photo of a sick houseplant and get an AI diagnosis and a care plan. $3.99/month subscription. Each diagnosis costs me about $0.03 in AI calls. Is this worth building?
evals.expected_output: Six verdicts with evidence; live keyword research (plant identification and care are crowded); money computed from the given cost; AI-content and saturated-category policy risks named.
assertions: An idea file is saved in outputs as markdown, with a verdict (go, maybe or no-go) for each of six criteria: demand, competition gap, money, stack fit, policy risk and solo-build size
Each criterion's verdict comes with reasoning that cites specific evidence (a number, a named app, a named guideline or a named feature)
Demand and competition rest on keyword or store data fetched in this run (autocomplete suggestions or top-app ratings), not on general impressions
It does not reduce the idea to a single numeric score or average
The money verdict rests on explicit arithmetic: the net price after the store's cut compared with the cost per user per month
It names at least one store policy risk with the specific Apple guideline or Play policy and a compliance path

evals.prompt: Vet my app in this folder. Is it worth finishing and shipping?
evals.expected_output: Reads the codebase in the given folder to understand the app, states its price assumption, runs keyword research, scores six criteria. (Run it against any Expo project.)
assertions: An idea file is saved in outputs as markdown, with a verdict (go, maybe or no-go) for each of six criteria: demand, competition gap, money, stack fit, policy risk and solo-build size
Each criterion's verdict comes with reasoning that cites specific evidence (a number, a named app, a named guideline or a named feature)
Demand and competition rest on keyword or store data fetched in this run (autocomplete suggestions or top-app ratings), not on general impressions
It does not reduce the idea to a single numeric score or average
It describes the app from its code (its features, payments and integrations), not just from the folder name
It states the price model it assumed, since the person didn't give one

evals.prompt: Quick gut check before I start: an app that makes a brand-new AI video of your pet every single day from a photo you upload once. I'd sell it as a $9.99 lifetime unlock, no subscription. Worth building?
evals.expected_output: Money is a no-go: a one-time price for a cost that continues daily (AI video per day). Overall looping, not go. Since this is one-shot, it lists the questions it would ask with recommended answers instead of inventing the person's answers.
assertions: An idea file is saved in outputs as markdown, with a verdict (go, maybe or no-go) for each of six criteria: demand, competition gap, money, stack fit, policy risk and solo-build size
Each criterion's verdict comes with reasoning that cites specific evidence (a number, a named app, a named guideline or a named feature)
Demand and competition rest on keyword or store data fetched in this run (autocomplete suggestions or top-app ratings), not on general impressions
It does not reduce the idea to a single numeric score or average
Money is scored no-go because a one-time price can't cover a cost that continues every day
The overall verdict is not go: it's no-go or looping on money
For the no-go it offers concrete ways to fix it (for example a subscription, a cap, or a cheaper output) as questions or options with a recommendation, without pretending the person already chose one
